comments.author: @jckpn
comments.text:
Great video as always Wes.

Summary:
- The total GPT-4 model has around 1.8 trillion parameters with 120 layers
- It's made of 16 different models, each with ~110b parameters and trained for a specific task/field (a technique known as MoE or Mixture of Experts)
- ~55b parameters are used solely for 'attention', i.e. guiding the model to stay on the topic at hand
- They believe GPT-4 was trained on ~13 trillion tokens (~10 trillion words)
- Some of these tokens were re-used (twice, or four times if it was code-based), so the actual size of the dataset is unknown but probably several trillion tokens
- They fine-tuned the model using more specific data from OpenAI and ScaleAI
- It took ~2e25 FLOPS of compute to train, using ~25k A100 processors for around 3 months
- GPT-4 is about 3x as computationally expensive to run than GPT-3.5
- It's thought a faster/cheaper model takes over after the first few words of a response, which could explain the complaints that ChatGPT got worse over time

This is all according to SemiAnalysis who published the information on their site behind a ~$500 paywall, but Yam Peleg released it for free on Twitter (now deleted).

comments.author: @Multihuntr0
comments.text:
*With regards to batch size*
When training a neural network, the steps are, roughly: 1. forward, 2. backward and 3. update. So, you push a batch of examples through your network (forward), you calculate how to get a better answer next time (backward), and then you update all of the weights just a tiny bit (update). This is how the machine "learns". 

Generally, having a large batch size is a good idea because it means that your backward pass, the part that calculates how to do better next time, is based on more information. Consider a tiny batch size: if you see a sentence "the cat flew through the air on it's wings", that's not a normal sentence - we don't want to associate wings with cats like that - but if you use that to train your model and you have a small batch size, that's going to be a really important data point the model will reference. Having a large batch size means that the model sees a lot more at once before each update step, and thus each update is more reliable. 

Typical batch sizes for small models are around 64-256. Recently batch sizes of 1024-8096 have been used for particularly large models and big training setups. The downside, however, is that if you have very large batch sizes, it takes longer for your model to learn. It would be like that person who can only read the theory and never tries to put it into practice. They don't try to learn very often, even though they have read a lot. So we want a balance, look at a lot, then try it, look at a lot, then try it. If you have 1000 GPUs, then this doesn't matter as much; you can just make it learn for longer to make up for it.

When counting the number of elements in a batch, typically you would count how many distinct examples there are. Notice that the person you are quoting says to not believe the fake numbers. They're referring to the fact that a single example in this case is actually many tokens. In this case, 8k tokens for most of the time, but 32k tokens by the end of training. So how many examples are there?

60 million tokens spread across 16 experts.
7.5 million tokens per expert (looks like every example was given to two experts)
32k tokens per context => approx. 234 contexts per batch.
8k tokens per context => approx. 937 contexts per batch.

That's not that many examples, but the context size is huge, so it makes sense the batch size would be smaller. 

*With regards to using copyrighted data*
In these discussions about AI ethics, it's good to inspect first principles. As I see it, these are the basic arguments: 
On the for side - which you present here - it is said "well, this AI learns like a human, and it wouldn't be illegal for a human to do it, so it should be legal". 
On the against side it is said "it doesn't matter how the AI does it, it will cause harm to people to let it continue, so it should be illegal".
My perspective is that there's a fundamental difference between these two positions on the nature of what is considered fair. On the "for" side, the fundamental point is that we should treat everyone equally. We can just think of the AI as something to be treated equally to a human. On the against side, the fundamental point is that everyone should be free to pursue whatever they like. Fairness is when people can do what they want to (so long as it doesn't hurt others). So, if many people are hurt by some actions, then it is definitionally unfair. 
I ummed and ahhed about it when generative AI first came out, because the "it does it like a human" line of reasoning is fairly sound. But the more I thought about it, the more I realised that it doesn't matter. Ignoring real outcomes for real people is always bad. How you choose to justify ignoring those outcomes is immaterial. Laws should serve humans, not the other way around.

A batch is how many, in this case tokens, go through the model before they adjust weights to min the loss.
For e.g. if you said "The dog barked at the", and the model came back with "sky", you can say "no, it should have been cat", now adjust weights so that it favors cat over sky. With batching you are giving the model more examples, add up and average all the weight changes, change once and go again. See if it does better. If you to adjust weights on every try it can skew things the wrong way. Batching allows a more smooth learning experience.

I didn't watch the entire video, kinda skipped around, so let me know if you covered this, but regarding the copyright you're not entirely right afaik. Yes, you can use any data to train the model, that part is correct, but there was a new copyright law passed regarding generated content, at least images, but I think it applies to everything, that specifies how the content can be used. In short, you can't copyright content generated by image generators, and you don't own them unless you perform transformative work on them yourself. Which means you can't just click "generate" and then claim you own that art or that you made it... but you can press "generate" and then paint over it, use it in some other transformative way, cut it up and mash it together with other generated or real art and so on... then you can claim copyright on the result... For example if you make a game with purely generated art, you can copyright the game and the ideas, but you can't copyright the art inside of it unless you made or modified that art.

and secondary, ofc, with everything you generate from a model that uses copyrighted material (which is pretty much all of it, as in the US  at least afaik you get a default copyright on anything you make even without registering) You have to check yourself if the generated result is violating any copyrights... for example if you generate a picture of mario, you definitely can't claim to own the copyright for mario... but this also applies to all lesser known artists.. so if your model happens to generate an exact copy, or close enough copy of someone elses art, then they still hold copyright to the intellectual property depicted. They don't own copyright over the actual image, as that was generated, but neither do you until you edit it...

long story short, copyrights are complex as fuck, and people that want to be using the models should at least have a surface level understanding of it, otherwise you're going to be very surprised when you make something using AI, and then you find out that it's nor protected and not really yours, and that someone else can do whatever they want with it completely legally, because you just pressed a button, and that simply doesn't count as making something. I think if you went to court over generated piece of text, story, code or music, you're probably going to be held accountable following the same law I just mentioned, as that is the best specified law we have over AI generated content right now...
